reading.body:
Nonprofit AI adoption is measured by sector research organizations, not a real-time registry, and the binding constraint is governance capacity rather than compute or power.

The seven sources split the problem into distinct angles. CEP and NTEN survey how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. The AI Equity Project tracks access and training gaps. Candid tracks grantmaking for AI adoption and technology infrastructure. Census BTOS includes nonprofit-heavy service sectors in its adoption series, and Stanford HAI reports macro social impact. No single entity maintains a real-time registry.

The practical uses named are grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets. Because governance capacity is the stated constraint, AI scaling in this sector is limited by oversight and policy adoption, not by access to compute or grid power. The data does not support a compute or power constraint for nonprofits.

The data does not provide adoption rates, budget figures, or compute and power requirements. It identifies who publishes sector research, not how many nonprofits have deployed AI or what infrastructure they use.

summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey is the only measured adoption figure in this material, and it does not isolate nonprofits. The latest reading for Other services, NAICS 81, which includes grantmaking and civic organizations, is 15.0% of firms answering yes to whether they used AI in the last two weeks, compared with 13.7% in the prior period. The series first asked the question in September 2023, and the Census Bureau notes that some values are suppressed. That 15.0% is a proxy for the sector rather than a number specific to nonprofits, and readers should treat it that way.

On what AI is actually used for, the harvested pages are thinner than the point list. CEP, the Center for Effective Philanthropy, is described as examining how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications, though the page text captured here shows only a headline about a participatory grantmaking model. NTEN, the Nonprofit Technology Network, runs regular sector wide research on technology investment, digital maturity, and AI policy adoption among nonprofits, and its page frames nonprofit technology as marked by inequities within organizations and within the sector.

The AI Equity Project addresses the access side. It describes structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs, turning public libraries and community spaces into learning environments that bring senior citizens and student volunteers together around practical AI tools. It operates as a global network with standardized technical curricula and training assets for underrepresented communities, and it runs the International AI for Impact Challenge, where top participants secure engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advisement. NTEN's material points the same direction, with an Equity Guide pledge and recognition for open source tools that nonprofit and advocacy groups can put to use.

Candid covers the funding side, providing grants and nonprofit data, and its page emphasizes transparency in grantmaking and the need for continued unrestricted support. It also notes that impact evaluations are becoming more important for both nonprofits and funders. The excerpt does not quantify how much grantmaking is directed toward AI adoption or technology infrastructure, so no figure can be given here.

The World of AI's own ecosystem page catalogues four individually verified organizations under nonprofits and open source foundations, two nonprofits and two open source foundations, each with a sourced classification note. LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform the broader AI community uses to benchmark model quality. Khan Academy is described as an end user of AI capability in education rather than a producer of it. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software that AI generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with. The page states plainly what it does not cover: no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data center specifications, and no open model foundations releasing weights. The notes confirm organizational structure and nonprofit status only, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a narrow set of conclusions. Adoption in the closest measured sector sits at 15.0%, so this is not a sector where AI use is universal. The constraint named in this page's own scope is governance capacity on small budgets, and the sources that speak to capability, NTEN and the AI Equity Project, frame the problem as equitable access and skills rather than tool selection. Stanford HAI's AI Index is cited as the citable macro series on AI's social impact and implementation across mission driven and public sector organizations, though no excerpt from it appears in this material. Where the sources are silent, on ROI figures, on vendor concentration, and on regulatory posture specific to nonprofits, nothing here should be inferred.

https://cep.org/.brief: The page from the Center for Effective Philanthropy features an article by Kevin Bolduc, who is identified as vice president of assessment and advisory services. The article’s title asks how one collaborative’s movement-led participatory model makes a difference for grantees. The harvested text does not include any further details or findings.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid says it provides comprehensive grants and nonprofit data to help users find funding, research nonprofits, and connect with funders. The page also notes that donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities. According to the text, this means many donors will never see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project reports that it develops structured educational routes and cross-generational initiatives aimed at making AI usable, ethical, and practical for every community. It says it converts public libraries and local community venues into hands-on learning settings where older adults and student volunteers jointly try out practical AI tools. The organization also describes a worldwide network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented groups, with support structures meant to ensure each student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. Its International AI for Impact Challenge asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world issues, and top entrants receive engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: This page catalogues four individually verified organisations ,  two nonprofits and two open-source foundations ,  whose roles touch AI tooling and evaluation, though the page states none are infrastructure builders in the compute-or-power sense. It describes LMSYS as the most directly AI-central entry, stewarding the Chatbot Arena evaluation platform used by the wider AI community to benchmark model quality, while characterising Khan Academy as an end-user of AI in education rather than a producer of it. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation are described as stewards of creative software that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with, with missions the page says predate and are not defined by AI. The page also flags what its data omits: no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights publicly, with the notes confirming only organisational structure and nonprofit status rather than funding scale, compute access or governance detail.
